title: The Grandparent Voice Clone
content:
Your phone rings. It sounds exactly like your child, grandchild or friend. They are crying and need money urgently.

Scammers can now copy a person's voice with AI tools, using a short recording — for example a voice note or a video posted online. The fake voice can sound very real.

Why it works: we trust the voices of people we love, and panic stops us thinking.

How to stay safe:

→ Hang up and call the person back on the number you already have saved

→ Ask a question only the real person would know

→ Agree a family "safe word" now, before anything happens

→ Remember that video calls and voice notes can also be faked with AI — calling back on a saved number is the safest check

→ Never send money while someone is rushing you

Real emergencies can wait one minute while you check. Scammers need you to act now.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The "Wrong Number" Long Con
content:
A message arrives from a stranger: "Hi, is this Ama? Sorry, wrong number." It looks harmless.

Sometimes it is a real mistake. But scammers also use this trick to start a chat. If you reply, they stay friendly, chat for days or weeks, and build trust. Later comes the ask: money for an emergency, a fee for a parcel, or an "investment" that pays big.

How to protect yourself:

→ You don't have to reply to a number you don't know

→ Be careful when a stranger keeps chatting after a "wrong number"

→ Never send money or codes to someone you have only met by text

→ Be very careful when a new "friend" starts talking about investments or crypto

→ Block and report numbers that keep pushing

A stranger who is still chatting weeks later and then talks about money is not a friend. It is a plan.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The Fake Streaming Fix
content:
Your favourite show keeps buffering. You search online for a fix and find a site offering an app that will "boost" your streaming.

Be careful. Fake help sites can appear high in search results, and the app they offer can be harmful — it may steal passwords, show you endless ads or take control of your device.

How to stay safe:

→ Only install apps from the Google Play Store or Apple App Store

→ For help, use the official app or website of the service — type the address yourself

→ Never install an app or give someone remote access because a website told you to

→ Ask someone you trust before installing anything new

Try the simple fixes first: restart your router and your device, move closer to the Wi-Fi, or check whether your data has run out.

Don't let a fake fix become a real problem.

title: The Fake Tech Support Pop-up
content:
A message suddenly fills your computer screen: "Your computer is infected! Call this number now!" It may beep, flash, or seem to lock your screen.

It is fake. Real warnings from Microsoft, Apple or Google do not ask you to phone a number shown in a pop-up. The people who answer are scammers. They ask you to install a "remote access" app so they can "fix" things. Once connected, they can steal passwords, open your banking, or demand payment for a fake repair.

How to stay safe:

→ Never call a number shown in a pop-up

→ Close the browser. If it won't close, restart the computer

→ Never let a stranger who contacted you connect to your computer

→ If you need help, contact the maker or the shop yourself, using the number on their official website

→ If you already let them in: disconnect from the internet, change your passwords from another device, and call your bank

Real support does not come looking for you. When something feels urgent, slow down.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The MoMo "Send It Back" Reversal Trick
content:
Someone calls in a panic: they sent MoMo to your number "by mistake" and beg you to send it back.

Often the "you have received" SMS is fake — no money ever entered your wallet. If you "return" it, you are sending your own money to a scammer.

How to stay safe:

→ Don't trust the SMS alone. Check your real balance: dial *170# (MTN), *110# (Telecel Cash), or open your official MoMo app

→ If your balance did not go up, it is a scam. Block the number

→ If money truly arrived by mistake, tell the caller to report it to their network's customer care, so the network handles the reversal

→ Never share your MoMo PIN or any code with a caller

→ Pressure to act fast is the biggest warning sign

A real mistake is fixed through the network — not by you sending money to a stranger.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The Fake "Confirm Your Payment" Invoice
content:
You get an SMS or email: "Your order is ready — pay GH₵ 89 here to confirm delivery." The logo looks like a company you know. The link looks official.

It's a scam. Criminals copy the look of real companies — shops, banks, delivery services, mobile networks — and send fake "invoices" or "confirm payment" links. The link opens a fake page that takes your card details or MoMo PIN. Some links try to install harmful apps.

How to stay safe:

→ Check the sender carefully — a random number or an odd email address is a warning sign

→ Never pay through a link in a message. Open the company's real app, or type their website yourself

→ Call the company on the number shown on their official website — not the number in the message

→ If you are unsure, ask someone you trust before paying

Urgent and official-looking is exactly how this scam works. When in doubt, check first.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The Fake Verification Badge Message
content:
You get a message that looks like it's from Facebook or Meta: "Your page will lose its blue badge. Verify your account now." There's a link.

It's a trick. The link opens a fake login page. When you type your password, the scammer takes over your account — and then your page, your contacts and sometimes your money.

How to stay safe:

→ Never click a "verification" link sent in a message or from a page you don't know

→ To check your account, open the Facebook app yourself and look in Settings

→ Turn on two-factor authentication (an extra code when you log in)

→ If you already typed your password, change it at once and remove any email or phone number you don't recognise

Anyone who wants your login wants everything behind it. Don't hand it over.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The Fake QR Code Sticker
content:
QR codes are now on shop counters, posters, menus and flyers. Scan, pay, done.

But a QR code is just a link you can't read with your eyes. A scammer can stick their own code over the real one, or print a flyer with a code that leads to a fake website asking for your card details, MoMo number or PIN.

How to protect yourself:

→ Before you confirm a payment, check that the name on your screen is the real shop's name

→ Look for a sticker placed on top of another one, or a code that looks freshly taped

→ After scanning, look at the web address. If a website asks for your PIN or password, stop

→ If in doubt, ask the seller for their merchant number and type it in yourself

→ Don't scan QR codes in random messages promising gifts or free data

Look before you pay.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The Delivery Fee Text Message
content:
You get a text: "Your parcel could not be delivered. Pay a small fee to reschedule." There's a link.

Scammers send the same message to thousands of numbers using the names of courier and delivery companies. Many people really are expecting a parcel, so it feels real. The link leads to a fake page that steals your card details, MoMo number or login.

The Cyber Security Authority has warned the public about fake parcel delivery and clearance messages with phishing links.

How to stay safe:

→ Don't click links in unexpected delivery texts

→ Check your order inside the shop's or courier's official app, or type their website yourself and enter your tracking number

→ Call the company on the number on their official website, not one in the message

→ Delete the text and report it

When in doubt, check it yourself — never through the link.

Report scams to the Cyber Security Authority: call or text 292, or WhatsApp 0501603111.

title: The "Look Who Died" Facebook Message
content:
A message arrives from a friend's account: "Look who just died" or "Is this you in this video?" There's a link.

It's a scam. Criminals take over accounts or create fake ones, then send these messages to everyone on the friend list. The shock makes you click. The link may:

→ Show a fake login page that steals your password

→ Try to install a harmful app

→ Ask you to "verify" your account with personal details

What to do:

→ If a message is shocking and comes with a mystery link, don't click it

→ Call or text your friend another way to ask if they sent it

→ Report the message to Facebook

→ If you already clicked and typed your password, change it immediately and turn on two-factor authentication

Real news doesn't hide behind a mystery link. Let curiosity wait.
